strengths: First post-training quantization (PTQ) work specifically tailored for Visual Geometry Grounded Transformers (VGGTs) or similar 3D foundation models, which is timely given their high computational demands.

Excellent empirical analysis identifying the root causes of quantization difficulties in VGGTs: specifically, the extreme outliers caused by data-independent special tokens (camera and register tokens), and the calibration instability arising from 3D multi-view data.

The proposed Dual-Smoothed Fine-Grained Quantization (DSFQ) elegantly combines pre-global Hadamard rotation with post-local channel smoothing in the rotated space, successfully mitigating both global heavy-tailed activations and local channel variance.

The Noise-Filtered Diverse Sampling (NFDS) strategy cleverly leverages the frame-relative inductive bias of multi-view 3D transformers to cluster similarity metrics, ensuring a representative and stable calibration set.

Outstanding performance on low-bit settings (W4A4), vastly outperforming established LLM and vision transformer PTQ baselines (such as Quarot, SmoothQuant, and GPTQ) with negligible overhead, verified on actual hardware with 2.5x speedup and 3.7x compression.
weaknesses: The core primitives of DSFQ (Hadamard rotation and channel-wise scaling) are adapted from prior LLM quantization literature (e.g., SmoothQuant, QuaRot), meaning the algorithmic novelty of these individual components is somewhat incremental.

The evaluation is restricted solely to the VGGT-1B model. Demonstrating the applicability of QuantVGGT (especially the calibration sampling strategy) to similar models such as DUSt3R or MASt3R would further bolster the generalizability claims.

Minor notation inconsistency in Equation 6: the scale factor is defined as $\hat{c}_i$ but written as $\hat{c}$ inside the diagonal matrix without explicit dimension mapping, which could be clarified.

strengths: First systematic investigation of Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) specifically designed for Visual Geometry Grounded Transformers (VGGT), which represent the state-of-the-art in learning-based 3D reconstruction.

Clear and well-founded identification of the main challenges of quantizing VGGTs, specifically how data-independent tokens (camera and register tokens) cause highly skewed, heavy-tailed activation distributions.

Innovative combination of global pre-rotation (Hadamard transform) and local post-smoothing (channel-scaling in the rotated space) to effectively mitigate extreme outlier values without introducing runtime overhead.

Novel Noise-Filtered Diverse Sampling (NFDS) calibration dataset construction strategy. It cleverly exploits the multi-view relative frame relation (inductive bias of VGGT) to form representative calibration clusters and filters out deep-layer activation outliers.

Excellent experimental results under low-bit settings (especially W4A4), where QuantVGGT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art PTQ methods (e.g., Quarot, SmoothQuant, GPTQ) and maintains ~98% of the full-precision counterpart performance, while delivering substantial hardware acceleration (2.5x) and memory savings (3.7x).
weaknesses: The individual techniques used in the quantization architecture (Hadamard rotation, channel-wise scaling) are largely derived from existing works like Quarot and SmoothQuant. Although their specific integration and application sequence (pre-rotation and post-scaling) is well-justified, the technical novelty of these individual blocks is somewhat incremental.

The generalization of the proposed methods to other models in the same family (such as DUSt3R or MASt3R) is not empirically demonstrated. Showing that the framework also works on these related models would further strengthen the claims of the paper.

Some clarification is needed for Equation (11) regarding how the feature matrix $A^i$ is reshaped into the frame-wise vectors $a^i_t \in \mathbb{R}^{\hat{d}}$. It would be helpful to explicitly define whether $a^i_t$ is the concatenated or flattened spatial tokens of frame $t$.

There is a minor discrepancy in the nomenclature of the ablation figures (Figure 5 vs. Figure 8), where the best-performing sampling strategy is labeled as 'NFDS' in one and 'Frame' in the other. Standardizing the terminology would improve readability.

strengths: First systematic investigation of Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) specifically tailored for Visual Geometry Grounded Transformers (VGGTs), which is a timely and practical contribution given the 1.2B parameter scale of these models.

Clear and detailed analysis of why standard PTQ fails on VGGT, pointing out that (1) data-independent camera/register tokens cause extreme outlier activations, and (2) multi-view training data makes calibration sets highly unstable.
The proposed Dual-Smoothed Fine-Grained Quantization (DSFQ) effectively combines global Hadamard rotation with post-local channel smoothing, showing strong theoretical and empirical motivation.
The Noise-Filtered Diverse Sampling (NFDS) introduces an interesting frame-aware similarity clustering to exploit the inductive biases of multi-view 3D models for stable calibration.

Impressive empirical results: under the challenging W4A4 quantization, QuantVGGT significantly outperforms standard baselines (e.g., maintaining 98% accuracy on Co3Dv2 while Quarot drops heavily), and achieves real-hardware speedup (2.5x) and memory savings (3.7x).
weaknesses: The core quantization techniques used (Hadamard rotation and channel smoothing) are largely adapted from prior works like SmoothQuant and QuaRot. The conceptual novelty of combining these two components is somewhat incremental.

The methodology is highly specific to the VGGT architecture (such as focusing heavily on camera/register tokens and frame-relative relationships). It is unclear how well the proposed framework generalizes to other popular 3D reconstruction models (e.g., DUSt3R, MASt3R) or other multi-view transformers.
Theorem 3.2 and its proof in the appendix feel somewhat over-formalized to justify a relatively intuitive clustering and uniform sampling strategy.
There are minor notation inconsistencies; for example, the definition of scale S in Figure 2's diagram does not perfectly align with the formulation of hat_c_i in Equation (6).

strengths: First systematic work on post-training quantization (PTQ) of Visual Geometry Grounded Transformers (VGGT), filling an important gap in compressing large-scale 3D foundation models.

Deep analysis of the unique quantization bottlenecks in VGGT, such as the extreme activation outliers caused by special camera/register tokens, and the multi-view calibration data selection challenge.

Well-designed methodology: Dual-Smoothed Fine-Grained Quantization (DSFQ) elegantly mitigates outlier-induced quantization errors, and Noise-Filtered Diverse Sampling (NFDS) leverages the frame-relation inductive bias of VGGT to construct a representative calibration set.

Excellent and extensive evaluation across multiple tasks (camera pose estimation, point map estimation, point cloud reconstruction) and datasets (CO3Dv2, DTU, 7-Scenes, NRGBD) showing state-of-the-art low-bit quantization results.
Real hardware speedup and memory compression results are demonstrated using CUTLASS on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, proving the practical value of the proposed method.
weaknesses: The conceptual components of DSFQ (Hadamard rotation from QuaRot and channel-wise smoothing from SmoothQuant) are adapted from prior LLM quantization work, which slightly limits the algorithmic novelty.
Theorem 3.2 and its proof are quite straightforward (standard maximum entropy of uniform distributions), offering limited new theoretical insights.

The evaluation focuses heavily on VGGT (with Fast3R briefly explored in the appendix). Demonstrating the applicability of the proposed methods on other categories of 3D vision transformers (e.g., 3D object detection or point cloud transformers) would further strengthen the generalizability claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely topic: the post-training quantization (PTQ) of large-scale 3D reconstruction transformers (VGGTs), which suffer from high memory and latency costs during deployment.

The empirical results are comprehensive and show substantial improvements in accuracy metrics (e.g., AUC for camera pose estimation and ACC for point map estimation) under low-bit widths (W4A4) compared to generic LLM/ViT quantization baselines like SmoothQuant and QuaRot.

The paper includes real hardware latency measurements on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, demonstrating that the proposed method can achieve a 2.5x speedup and 3.7x memory reduction with minimal runtime overhead.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is limited. The Dual-Smoothed Fine-Grained Quantization (DSFQ) is a relatively straightforward combination of two well-established techniques: pre-global Hadamard rotation (from QuaRot/QuIP) and channel-wise scaling (from SmoothQuant). Applying SmoothQuant scaling in the rotated space is a incremental engineering extension rather than a fundamental methodological breakthrough.

Theorem 3.2 and its proof are mathematically trivial. It is well known from standard information theory that the uniform distribution maximizes Shannon entropy over a finite discrete set. Presenting this basic textbook concept as a novel 'Calibration sampling principle' (Theorem 3.2) adds little value and appears overly decorated.

The Noise-Filtered Diverse Sampling (NFDS) pipeline relies on several heuristic steps (outlier filtering using deep-layer statistics, frame-aware correlation vector computation, and K-Means clustering) that introduce multiple hyperparameters ($p$, $K$, threshold $T$). While sensitivity analyses are provided, the complexity of this calibration pipeline reduces the elegance and simplicity of the PTQ process.

There are several typos and formatting errors throughout the text. For example, 'Krishnamoorthi, 1806' is cited on pages 3 and 4, which is an obvious typo for 2018. Additionally, the word 'diversed' is repeatedly used (e.g., in Figure 2 and Theorem 3.2) instead of the correct English word 'diverse'.

The evaluation is largely limited to a narrow scope of models (VGGT and Fast3R), making it unclear if the calibration sampling strategies generalize well to other multi-view or spatial-temporal vision transformer architectures.

strengths: First systematic study and specialized post-training quantization (PTQ) framework for Visual Geometry Grounded Transformers (VGGTs), targeting the unique challenges of 3D foundation models.

Well-motivated and effective technical solutions: Dual-Smoothed Fine-Grained Quantization (DSFQ) to resolve outlier issues caused by data-independent register/camera tokens, and Noise-Filtered Diverse Sampling (NFDS) to stabilize calibration under multi-view 3D data.

Impressive performance in low-bit scenarios: W4A4 quantization achieves nearly lossless performance (retaining over 98% accuracy of the FP16 model), significantly outperforming generic SOTA quantization methods like QuaRot and SmoothQuant.
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks (CO3Dv2, DTU, 7-Scenes, NRGBD) along with actual hardware implementation showing 2.5x speedup and 3.7x memory reduction on an RTX 4090.
weaknesses: The core components of DSFQ heavily build upon existing techniques, specifically Hadamard rotation from QuaRot and channel-wise smoothing from SmoothQuant, limiting the purely conceptual novelty of the quantization architecture.

The frame-aware clustering in NFDS assumes a specific multi-view sequential structure (relative relationship between the first frame and subsequent frames), which is tailored to VGGT/Fast3R and may not directly generalize to other 3D representation formats (e.g., NeRFs, 3D Gaussians, or single-view architectures).
